# FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection

Shaswata Mitra¹, Subash Neupane², Martin Duclos³, Sudip Mittal⁴,  
Aritran Piplai⁵, Md Rayhanur Rahman⁶, Edward Zieglar⁷ Shahram Rahimi⁸
Affiliation: ²Meharry Medical College – {²subash.neupane@mmc.edu}  
⁵The University of Texas at El Paso – ⁵apiplai@utep.edu  
¹³⁴⁶⁸The University of Alabama  
{¹smitra3, ³ mjduclos, ⁴sudip.mittal, ⁶mdrayhanur.rahman,
⁸shahram.rahimi}@ua.edu  
⁷National Security Agency – ⁷evziegl@uwe.nsa.gov

###### Abstract

Signature-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) detect malicious
activity by matching network or host events against predefined rules.
Security analysts manually develop these rules from Cyber Threat
Intelligence (CTI). As threats evolve, this manual pipeline faces two
bottlenecks. Before authoring a new rule, an analyst must reconcile the
incoming CTI with the existing rule base and determine whether to
create, update, or retire one. This process is challenging due to the
representational differences between the CTI and Rule formats. This gap
limits the effectiveness of keyword- and embedding-based search, making
rule reconciliation cognitively demanding and, in turn, contributing to
‘‘rule bloat’’. Second, automated verification of a new rule is
inherently difficult as zero-day threats lack ground truth from
simulated testing. Hence, standard metrics cannot prove that a rule
semantically adheres to the CTI, and the use of LLMs leads to
non-deterministic behavior. To address these challenges, we introduce
FALCON ¹¹ 1 Code & Dataset:
[github.com/shaswata09/falcon](https://github.com/shaswata09/falcon), an
agentic framework for CTI-grounded rule retrieval, generation, and
validation. At its core, a novel CTI-Rule semantic scorer²² 2 Models:
[huggingface.co/collections/shaswatamitra/falcon](https://huggingface.co/collections/shaswatamitra/falcon),
quantifies the functional alignment between a CTI and a rule; the same
signal drives a retriever that surfaces relevant deployed rules and a
ground-truth-free validator that scores generated ones. Around it, a
generation pipeline produces deployable rules from CTI in real time and
refines them through self-reflective syntactic, semantic, and
performance validators. Across network (Snort) and host-based (YARA)
platforms on a purpose-built CTI-Rule dataset, FALCON attains a mean
relevance of $`\approx`$0.72, with 84% inter-rater agreement among
cybersecurity analysts, underscoring the promise of real-time security
automation.

###### Index Terms: 

Cybersecurity, Intrusion Detection Systems, Automated Rule Generation,
Large Language Models, Agentic AI

## I Introduction

Every year, approximately 7 trillion intrusion attempts are made
globally, with over 90% of breaches exploiting known, unpatched
vulnerabilities  \[cybersecurity_stat\]. Signature-based Intrusion
Detection Systems (IDSs) counter such threats by continuously monitoring
networks and hosts and matching activity against predefined rules that
encode attack signatures and behaviors. Security Operations Center (SOC)
analysts are responsible for developing these rules through a structured
rule generation process. This process involves several phases, including
retrieving relevant deployed rules, analyzing threat behavior,
generating rules, and assessing their compatibility with the existing
rule base. This process is iterative, where findings are accumulated in
Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) to enable optimal rule generation. This
IDS rule-generation process from CTI is consistent across network and
host media and mainly relies on analyst expertise to ensure optimal rule
generation.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/tldr_overview.png)

Fig. 1: TLDR; FALCON accepts CTI and deployed IDS rules, produces an IDS
rule and analyst note for explainability. The rule is generated through
orchestration of a Rule Retriever, LLM based Generator, and a
deterministic Validator.

This manual, cognitively heavy pipeline struggles to keep pace with a
fast-evolving threat landscape. As attackers vary their Tactics,
Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs), new signatures, behaviors, and
matching rules proliferate. In contrast, existing rules
decay \[chinwe2025adversarial\], and the daily volume of CTI, including
sandbox traces, behavioral logs, and IoCs, makes manual analysis
burdensome and cognitively demanding \[wack2002guidelines\]. Two
problems make this especially hard to automate. First, a new rule cannot
be generated in isolation: the analyst must search through the deployed
rule base for functionally relevant rules and decide whether to create,
update, or deprecate one. Skipping this reconciliation inflates the rule
base (‘rule-bloat’), straining IDS engine performance and functionality,
yet performing it demands expertise and assumes relevant rules are
retrieved beforehand to enable context-aware generation. The
representational gap between natural language or structured CTI and
formal rule syntax causes keyword and embedding-similarity search to
fail at exactly this retrieval. Second, without ground truth, it is
difficult to deterministically determine whether an LLM-generated rule
meets the functional requirements of the CTI \[jin2024simllm\], as it is
challenging to simulate and test zero-day threats. Hence, any delay or
error in deployment leaves systems exposed without any defense.

IDS rules are also platform-dependent. Network rules such as Snort
detect and block malicious traffic, whereas host rules such as YARA flag
system-level anomalies, for example memory or registry changes, by
matching textual or binary patterns. Covering both demands rules
tailored to each platform’s capabilities, compounding the manual
effort \[bridges2019survey\]. Accordingly, we ask the following research
questions (RQs):

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To address these challenges, we present FALCON (Feedback-driven
ALignment framework for Cti-to-rule generatiON), a self-reflective
agentic framework for IDS rule generation and improvement. FALCON builds
on AI-based signature and behavior extraction from threat
analysis \[guan2024logllm, mitra2024localintel, rahman2024chronocti\]
and uses agentic LLMs to automate the full pipeline: given a CTI input
of behavioral descriptions, signatures, or IoCs, it autonomously
produces deployable rules for the target environment
\[Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].
At its core, a novel CTI-to-Rule Semantic Scorer quantifies the
functional alignment between a CTI and a rule. The same signal drives
both a retriever that surfaces relevant deployed rules and a
deterministic validation pipeline that checks each generated rule for
syntactic correctness, semantic alignment, and performance for
self-reflection and explainability. This couples relevant rule reuse
with an approximation of test-time quality assessment, enabling adaptive
rule generation while curbing ‘rule bloat’.

Our contributions include:

- •
  A self-reflective framework that autonomously transforms heterogeneous
  CTI into deployable IDS rules across both network (Snort) and host
  (YARA) mediums (RQ-1).
- •
  A CTI-Rule semantic alignment model that quantifies the functional
  correspondence between a CTI and a formal rule without ground truth,
  and show that a single such model serves a dual role, retrieving
  relevant deployed rules and validating generated ones (RQ-2).
- •
  A self-reflective validation pipeline that diagnoses a candidate rule
  along syntactic, semantic, and performance dimensions and returns
  feedback, enabling an LLM agent to iteratively refine sub-optimal
  rules with measurable gains over one-shot generation (RQ-3).
- •
  A comprehensive dataset that mimics real-world scenarios, pairing
  ground-truth and relevant-but-outdated IDS rules with their
  corresponding CTIs, enabling both quantitative evaluation and
  qualitative expert validation of FALCON (RQ-1, 2, 3).

The remainder of the paper covers preliminaries
(Section [II](#S2 "II Preliminaries and Motivation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
problem formulation
(Section [III](#S3 "III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
the FALCON framework
(Section [IV](#S4 "IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
experiments and evaluation
(Section [V](#S5 "V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
and concluding remarks with future directions
(Section [VI](#S6 "VI Conclusion ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")).

## II Preliminaries and Motivation

### II-A From Hand-Crafted to LLM-Generated Rules

Automated signature generation predates LLMs by nearly two decades.
Classical NIDS methods derive signatures from honeypots or captured
traffic \[newsome2005polygraph, kreibich2004honeycomb\], and HIDS
methods build YARA rules from malware corpora using $`n`$-grams,
biclustering, or learned scorers \[raff2020autoyara, li2023packgenome,
naik2020evaluating, IEEE10693305\]. These operate on raw binaries or
pre-captured traffic and offer no mechanism to reconcile new rules
against a deployed rule base.

LLMs have shifted the input from raw artifacts toward analyst-facing
text, and a fast-growing line now synthesizes detection rules from cloud
OSCTI \[schwartz2024llmcloudhunter\], honeypot
PCAPs \[balasubramanian2024hex2sign\], package
metadata \[zhang2025rulellm\], proof-of-concept
exploits \[lian2025rulemaster\], ICS network
flows \[moreno2025leveraging\], or live attack traffic in a cyber
range \[du2025harnessing\], with recent multi-agent variants that
additionally repair rules against an existing ruleset to limit
redundancy \[li2025gridai\]; a parallel line curates deployed SIEM rule
sets post hoc \[shukla2025rulegenie\]. Across this work, two properties
recur: the input is typically an observable artifact rather than the
heterogeneous linguistic CTI analysts actually author, and each system
targets a single platform.

### II-B Open Gaps

Lack of deterministic assessment: Judging whether a generated rule is
functionally faithful to its CTI is mostly qualitative and relies on
analyst expertise and post-hoc trials. In contrast, quantitative
evaluations require information unavailable for novel threats.
Deployment-based evaluation replays labeled attack traffic in a live
engine \[li2025gridai, moreno2025leveraging, du2025harnessing\],
presuming the threat is already observable and thus cannot judge a rule
synthesized from scratch. Reference-based evaluation compares against a
held-out human rule using lexically incompatible metrics such as ROUGE
or BLEU \[wang2025rulepilot, bertiger2025evaluating\]. Furthermore,
LLM-as-judge \[guerdan2026validating\] scoring offers no calibrated,
reproducible signal. The field thus lacks a way to quantify, without
ground truth, how well a generated rule captures its CTI.

No paired CTI-to-rule corpus exists: Detection rules (e.g., Snort, YARA)
and CTI reports are each abundant but siloed, and the
CTI-narrative-to-rule mapping that analysts produce by hand or
automatically is not recorded in any public dataset. The artifacts prior
to the generator’s release are bound to a different input or a single
platform: RuleLLM \[zhang2025rulellm\] open-sources tooling over package
code, LLMCloudHunter \[schwartz2024llmcloudhunter\] maps a small set of
cloud reports to Sigma, and Hex2Sign \[balasubramanian2024hex2sign\]
derives Suricata rules from honeypot PCAPs. At the same time,
substantive real-world corpora remain private \[li2025gridai\]. None
pairs analyst-authored CTI with deployable rules across both NIDS and
HIDS, and standard keyword or embedding similarity does not bridge the
representational gap between prose CTI and formal rule syntax.

The above-mentioned gaps shape FALCON. We
release[2](#footnote2 "footnote 2 ‣ Abstract ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection"),
to our knowledge, the first paired CTI-rule dataset spanning Snort and
YARA, augmented with relevant-but-outdated rules for retrieval, and a
learned CTI-Rule alignment scorer that supplies the missing fidelity
signal for both retrieval and validation. We formalize the problem in
Section [III](#S3 "III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").

## III Problem Formulation

| Notation                                                                | Description                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $`\emptyset`$                                                           | Null Set                                                      |
| $`\mathcal{I}`$                                                         | Generation Instruction (Constant)                             |
| $`\mathcal{T}`$                                                         | Validation Threshold (Constant)                               |
| $`\mathcal{E}_{c},\ \mathcal{E}_{r}`$                                   | CTI and Rule Embedding Encoders                               |
| $`\Phi(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R})`$                                       | CTI-Rule Alignment Scorer                                     |
| $`\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\mid\mathcal{C}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}\}`$                | Set of Cyber Threat Intelligence                              |
| $`\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}\in\mathcal{F}\}`$                | Set of Validation Feedback                                    |
| $`\{\mathcal{F}^{s},\mathcal{F}^{f},\mathcal{F}^{p},\mathcal{F}^{a}\}`$ | Syntax, Semantic, Performance, Analyst Feedback               |
| $`\{\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}\mid\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}\in\mathcal{R}\}`$        | Existing and Deployed IDS Rule Set                            |
| $`\{\mathcal{R}_{i}\mid\mathcal{R}_{i}\in\mathcal{R}\}`$                | Generated IDS Rule Set                                        |
| $`\epsilon\in[0,1]`$                                                    | Semantic Alignment Score ($`\mathcal{C}`$ vs $`\mathcal{R}`$) |

TABLE I: Description of Notation.

Threat signatures
$`\mathcal{S}=\{\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{S}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{S}_{n}\}`$
are identifiable static indicators of malicious activity, such as IP
addresses, hashes, or other Indicators of Compromise (IoCs). Threat
behaviors
$`\mathcal{B}=\{\mathcal{B}_{0},\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{n}\}`$
are dynamic patterns, such as protocol usage, file types, or signature
combinations that characterize malicious operations. A CTI instance
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ encapsulates structured or unstructured knowledge
containing signatures, behaviors, or both, and the corpus is
$`\mathcal{C}=\{\mathcal{C}_{0},\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{n}\}`$.

Hypothesis: We assume each CTI contains the relevant signatures and
behaviors
\[$`\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap(\mathcal{S}_{i}\cup\mathcal{B}_{i})\neq\emptyset`$\],
that is, it carries the information needed for rule generation. Without
this condition, FALCON cannot recover $`\mathcal{S}_{i}`$ and
$`\mathcal{B}_{i}`$ from $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ to contextualize against
the deployed rule base $`\mathcal{R}^{e}`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We decompose $`f`$ into three coupled sub-problems, aligned with our
RQ-1 to RQ-3.

(i) Functional alignment without ground truth (RQ-2). Since no reference
rule exists at test time, we require a deterministic, learned
quantitative scorer $`\Phi`$ that maps a CTI-rule pair to a bounded
alignment score,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\Phi:\ (\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R})\ \mapsto\ \epsilon\in[0,1],
``` |  | (2) |

with $`\epsilon\to 1`$ for functionally aligned pairs. $`\Phi`$ is the
only quality signal available for downstream evaluation. Hence, shared
by the next two sub-problems.

(ii) Context-aware retrieval and generation (RQ-1). Using $`\Phi`$,
FALCON retrieves the relevant deployed rules and records the strongest
existing match,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}=\underset{\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{R}^{e}}{\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k}\ \Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}),\qquad\epsilon_{i}^{\max}=\max_{\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}}\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}),
``` |  | (3) |

then generates a candidate conditioned on the CTI and this retrieved
context, $`\mathcal{R}_{i}=f(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i})`$.

(iii) Self-reflective refinement (RQ-3). The candidate is validated into
structured feedback
$`\mathcal{F}_{i}=\mathcal{F}^{s}_{i}\cup\mathcal{F}^{f}_{i}\cup\mathcal{F}^{p}_{i}`$,
whose semantic term $`\mathcal{F}^{f}_{i}`$ is derived from
$`\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i})`$. FALCON then refines
iteratively,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}=f\!\left(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{i}^{(t)}\right)\ \ \text{until}\ \ \mathcal{F}_{i}\geq\mathcal{T}\ \wedge\ \Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i})\geq\epsilon_{i}^{\max},
``` |  | (4) |

so that the accepted rule passes every validation phase and is more
aligned with $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ than the best retrieved rules.

Together, $`\Phi`$ links retrieval and validation through a single
ground-truth-free signal, while $`f`$ and the feedback loop realize
generation and refinement.
Section [IV](#S4 "IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")
instantiates each component.

Fig. 2: FALCON architecture, divided into Generation and Validation
phases. The Rule Generator produces a candidate IDS rule from the CTI
and retrieved rules, which is then validated for syntax, semantics, and
performance. The Orchestration Agent routes validation feedback and
triggers regeneration, and validated rules are reviewed by an analyst
before deployment.

## IV FALCON Framework

We first present the overall solution approach, then describe each
modules
\[Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
and finally walk through an end-to-end use case that generates an IDS
rule ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$) from a CTI ($`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$).

### IV-A Solution Approach

To test RQ-1, FALCON
\[Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\]
operates in two phases for autonomous IDS rule “generation” and
“validation”.

Input: Cyber Threat Intelligence ($`\mathcal{C}_{i})`$)

Output: Relevant IDS Rule
($`\mathcal{R}_{i}\leftarrow f(\mathcal{C}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}^{e}_{i})`$)

Generation Phase:

$`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}=\underset{\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{R}^{e}}{\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k}\ \Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R})\leftarrow find\_relevant\_rules(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R})`$

$`\epsilon_{i}^{max}=\max_{\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}}\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R})`$

$`\mathcal{R}_{i}\leftarrow generate\_rule(\mathcal{C}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}^{e}_{i},\ \emptyset)`$

$`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow execute\_validation(\mathcal{R}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}^{e}_{i},\ \epsilon_{i}^{max})`$

while *$`\mathcal{F}_{i}<\mathcal{T}`$* do

    $`\mathcal{R}_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{R}_{i+1}\leftarrow generate\_rule(\mathcal{C}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}^{e}_{i},\ \mathcal{F}_{i})`$

    $`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{F}_{i+1}\leftarrow execute\_validation(\mathcal{C}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}_{i},\ \epsilon_{i}^{max})`$

return $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$

Validation Phase \[$`execute\_validation`$\]:

$`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow\ \mathcal{F}_{i}^{s}\ \cup\ \mathcal{F}_{i}^{f}\ \cup\ \mathcal{F}_{i}^{p}\ \leftarrow\ \emptyset`$

$`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{F}_{i}^{s}\ \cup\ syntactic\_validator(\mathcal{R}_{i})`$

if *$`\mathcal{F}_{i}^{s}\ ==\ \texttt{False}`$* then

    return $`\mathcal{F}_{i}`$

else

    $`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{F}_{i}^{f}\ \cup\ semantic\_validator(\mathcal{C}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}_{i},\ \epsilon_{i}^{max})`$

    if
*$`\mathcal{F}_{i}^{f}<\epsilon_{i}^{max}\ \ \text{or}\ \ \mathcal{F}_{i}^{f}<\mathcal{T}^{f}`$*
then

        return $`\mathcal{F}_{i}`$

    else

        $`\mathcal{F}_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{F}_{i}^{p}\ \cup\ performance\_validator(\mathcal{R}_{i},\ \mathcal{R}^{e}_{i})`$

return $`\mathcal{F}_{i}`$

Algorithm 1 Orchestration Agent Pseudo-code

- –
  The Generation Phase begins with an input CTI ($`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$).
  FALCON first retrieves the deployed rules ($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$)
  relevant to $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ to contextualize generation, and
  records their maximum semantic score ($`\epsilon_{i}^{max}`$) for
  later validation. The Rule Generator LLM Agent is then invoked with
  the generation instruction ($`\mathcal{I}`$), $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$, and
  $`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$ to produce an initial candidate
  ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$), where $`\mathcal{I}`$ encodes the extraction
  methods and generation guidelines the agent must follow. The candidate
  passes to a chain of serial validators; whenever it fails the
  validation threshold ($`\mathcal{T}`$), the returned feedback
  ($`\mathcal{F}_{i}`$) drives iterative regeneration
  ($`\mathcal{R}_{i+1}`$) until all criteria are
  met \[sudarshan2024agentic\]. A SOC analyst finally reviews the
  validated rule, approves it for deployment, and retires outdated ones;
  the analyst may also supply structured or unstructured feedback
  ($`\mathcal{F}^{a}`$) to trigger regeneration, sustaining a real-time
  security posture.
- –
  The Validation Phase evaluates $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ through serial
  syntactic, semantic, and performance checks. The rule is first parsed
  for structural correctness; if valid, semantic analysis assesses its
  logical consistency and functional alignment with $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$,
  requiring a score higher than the best retrieved match; upon passing,
  performance validation confirms operational effectiveness, including
  reconciliation with existing rules ($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$), runtime
  efficiency, and reliability. Failure at any stage returns immediate
  feedback for targeted refinement in the next iteration.

### IV-B FALCON System Modules

#### IV-B1 Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) or $`\mathcal{C}`$

CTI is the primary input to FALCON. Extracted from threat reports or
logs, it comprises signatures ($`\mathcal{S}`$) and behaviors
($`\mathcal{B}`$), such as IP addresses, hashes, IoCs, and protocols,
forming the semantic basis for rule generation.

#### IV-B2 Relevant IDS Rule Retriever

The retriever identifies deployed rules ($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$)
relevant to $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$, supplying context that lets the Rule
Generator LLM Agent decide whether to author a new rule or update an
existing one. Because $`\mathcal{C}`$ and $`\mathcal{R}`$ have
dissimilar representations, traditional embedding cosine similarity
\[$`\text{sim}\!\left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{C}),\,\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{R}^{e})\right)\approx\epsilon\ |\ \epsilon\to 0`$\]
and keyword search (TF-IDF) both fail to capture functional relevance. A
dedicated retriever is therefore required to draw $`\mathcal{C}`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}`$ embeddings into a shared space for context-aware
retrieval.

#### IV-B3 Rule Generator LLM Agent

An LLM agent that generates $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ from
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$, $`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$, $`\mathcal{I}`$, and
$`\mathcal{F}_{i}`$, interpreting feedback to iteratively refine the
rule in the context of $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$.

#### IV-B4 Generated IDS Rule or $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$

The output of FALCON: an actionable rule that transforms
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ while accounting for existing rules
($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$), refined across iterations until all
validation passes.

#### IV-B5 Validator Feedback or $`\mathcal{F}`$

The report produced by the syntax, semantic, and performance validators
or the analyst. It serves two roles, evaluating $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$
against $`\mathcal{T}`$ and guiding subsequent generations, by pairing a
numeric value for thresholding with descriptive, unstructured guidance
for the Rule Generator LLM Agent and analyst.

#### IV-B6 Syntax Validator

Verifies that $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ conforms to the target engine’s
syntax, checking components such as headers, conditions, and options. On
error, it returns a negative binary (False) signal with the parser’s
error description for regeneration.

#### IV-B7 Semantic Validator

The Semantic Validator assesses whether $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ logically
captures $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$, e.g., protocols, payload signatures, and
behavioral patterns consistent with the detection objective. The
representational gap between heterogeneous language-formatted CTI and
formal rule syntax renders embedding-based similarity or existing
graph-matching approaches inapplicable. At the same time, direct LLM
judgment is unreliable in first-shot inference due to
hallucination \[liu2024exploring\] and degraded long-context
performance \[liu2023your\]. Unlike code, a zero-day threat cannot be
simulated with mock test cases to verify functional alignment. We
therefore required a shared latent space that projects the logical
correspondence across representations, that is, in our case, between
$`\mathcal{C}`$ and $`\mathcal{R}`$. Hence, a bi/dual encoder is trained
to embed both into a cross-modal shared projection latent space for
similarity computation \[radford2021learning\]. We further detail our
model in
Section [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").

The resulting score feeds a Semantic Analysis LLM agent that, guided by
this quantified signal and structured prompts, predicts logical
inconsistencies in $`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$; such context-quantified guidance
has been shown to improve LLM reasoning and
reliability \[sudarshan2024agentic\]. For efficiency, we fold these
inconsistencies into the next regeneration run rather than emitting them
separately, since regeneration occurs only when the candidate is less
aligned than the retrieved rules
\[$`\epsilon_{i}^{\mathcal{R}_{i}}<\epsilon_{i}^{max}`$\] or below
threshold \[$`\epsilon_{i}^{\mathcal{R}_{i}}<\mathcal{T}`$\]. Because
the improvement-feedback tokens precede the next rule’s tokens, they set
the correct generation trajectory for $`\mathcal{R}_{i+1}`$ without
sacrificing accuracy, echoing chain-of-thought
prompting \[yao2023react\].

#### IV-B8 Performance Validator

The Performance Validator assesses the operational efficiency of
$`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ for a production environment. For example, matching
many signatures via sequential if-else logic is functional but inferior
to a shared regular expression. Such checks can use traditional
algorithms, such as DAG analysis \[abbes2010efficient, wang2023dag\], or
separate LLM inference; LLM agents have been adapted to evaluate
optimization criteria \[gao2024search\] accurately. For this work, we
adopt traditional validators with a lenient threshold to assess
execution speed, resource utilization, and rule reusability, with
detection coverage; rules with excessive latency, redundant logic, or
unnecessary additions are returned with negative feedback
($`\mathcal{F}^{p}`$). Since some existing rules can address a zero-day
with minimal change, each retrieved rule $`\mathcal{R}_{i}^{e}`$ is
assigned a CREATE, UPDATE, or DELETE label. Given the domain’s
sensitivity, where an erroneous deletion or addition is costly, these
labels are surfaced as an Analyst Note for SOC approval rather than
applied automatically, ensuring only high-performing, compatible rules
advance with accountability.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/semantic_scorer_model.png)

Fig. 3: Semantic Scorer training and execution diagram. A bi-encoder
model quantifies semantic similarity between $`\mathcal{C}`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}`$ on a \[0–1\] scale. Each $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ is encoded independently, and cosine similarity
populates the matrix. During contrastive pre-training, correct
$`(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i})`$ pairs (diagonal entries) are
optimized for the highest softmax score to capture logical alignment. At
execution, the trained model scores a new candidate rule
$`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ for semantic consistency w.r.t. the input CTI
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$.

### IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model

To answer RQ-2, we instantiate the scorer $`\Phi`$ of
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")).
Code-similarity models (GraphCodeBERT \[guo2020graphcodebert\],
CodeBERT \[feng2020codebert\]) capture structural equivalence but ignore
detection intent and rule syntax, and lexical metrics
(ROUGE \[lin2004rouge\], BLEU \[papineni2002bleu\]) miss the CTI–rule
relationship given their wide gap in length and abstraction. We instead
encode each input independently with
$`\mathcal{E}_{c},\mathcal{E}_{r}`$, giving
$`\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}=\mathcal{E}_{c}(\mathcal{C}_{i})`$,
$`\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{E}_{r}(\mathcal{R})\in\mathbb{R}^{768}`$
\[Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B8 Performance Validator ‣ IV-B FALCON System Modules ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
and score by a calibrated cosine,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R})=\sigma\!\big(\cos(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}},\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{R}})\big)=\epsilon\in[0,1].
``` |  | (5) |

Independent encoding keeps $`\Phi`$ cheap over the full base
$`\mathcal{R}^{e}`$ at retrieval and each refinement step. We evaluate
both bi- and dual-encoder configurations under contrastive fine-tuning
(below); both perform well in practice \[see repository
Appendix[1](#footnote1 "footnote 1 ‣ Abstract ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].

Latent regularization: A deterministic autoencoder is inadequate: its
reconstruction objective rewards modality-specific surface features, the
very cues separating $`\mathcal{C}`$ from $`\mathcal{R}`$, and its point
estimates leave a sparse, discontinuous latent where cosine is
unreliable and contrastive training collapses onto an anisotropic cone.
We thus use a VAE-style stochastic encoder
$`q(\mathbf{z}\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}(x),\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}(x))\big)`$,
$`x\in\{\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i}\}`$, reparameterized
$`\mathbf{z}=\boldsymbol{\mu}(x)+\boldsymbol{\sigma}(x)\odot\boldsymbol{\eta}`$,
$`\boldsymbol{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)`$, regularized to an isotropic
prior over the fixed $`768`$-dimensional latent,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\,D_{KL}\!\big(q(\mathbf{z}\mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)\big)
``` |  | (6) |

This fills latent holes (smooth, calibrated cosine geometry), injects
noise that resists collapse, and aligns the distributions
$`q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{C}_{i})`$ and
$`q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{R}_{i})`$ as overlapping clusters rather than
points, robust under limited data, yielding
$`\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{C}}\overset{\text{func}}{\leftrightarrow}\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}`$.

Contrastive fine-tuning (CFT): For a batch of $`N`$ pairs we minimize
the InfoNCE loss so the highest cosine falls on the diagonal
pair \[wu2021rethinking\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{contrastive}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp\!\big(\cos(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}},\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{R}_{i}})/\tau\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp\!\big(\cos(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}},\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{R}_{j}})/\tau\big)},
``` |  | (7) |

with temperature $`\tau`$ and full objective
$`\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{contrastive}}+\beta\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}`$
($`\beta`$-VAE \[burgess2018understanding\]). Minimizing it drives
$`\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i})\to 1`$ for aligned pairs and
$`\to 0`$ otherwise
\[Eq. ([5](#S4.E5 "In IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection"))\],
the $`\epsilon\to 1`$ desideratum of
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")).
Both bi- and dual-encoder configurations train well under CFT
\[Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ IV-D4 Semantic Validation ‣ IV-D FALCON Implementation and Module Interaction ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
with the bi-encoder (all-mpnet-base-v2³³ 3
huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2) performing
slightly better; we adopt it as the default $`\Phi`$, a single model
serving both retrieval
\[Eq. ([3](#S3.E3 "In III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection"))\]
and validation
\[Eq. ([4](#S3.E4 "In III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection"))\]
\[see
Appendices [I](#A9 "Appendix I Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Analysis ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")–[I-B](#A9.SS2 "I-B Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Validation ‣ Appendix I Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Analysis ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")
for further analysis\].

### IV-D FALCON Implementation and Module Interaction

To show FALCON in practice, we trace a YARA ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$)
generation use case from a CTI input ($`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$) through
validation.

#### IV-D1 CTI Ingestion and Rule Generation

The process begins with a CTI input of signatures and behavior
descriptors, e.g., a malware sample with known headers and behavior. The
Relevant IDS Rule Retriever surfaces semantically similar rules
($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$) via the semantic scorer and a preset
threshold. A one-shot generation prompt tailored to the target format
(e.g., Snort, YARA) combines $`\mathcal{I}`$, $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$, and
$`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$, and the Rule Generator LLM Agent emits a
candidate rule ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$). See Appendix
\[Box [F-B](#A6.SS2 "F-B Candidate Generation ‣ Appendix F Example End-to-End Rule Generation and Validation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\]
for full $`\mathcal{I}`$ and end-to-end use-case example.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### IV-D2 Generated IDS Rule

The agent’s output ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$) encodes the threat-prevention
logic derived from $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ and $`\mathcal{R}_{i}^{e}`$,
typically including protocol, domain-matching, and content-matching
elements. As an unvalidated candidate, it must pass syntactic, semantic
(functional), and performance checks plus SOC review before deployment.

#### IV-D3 Syntactic Validation

$`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$ is first sent to the Syntax Validator, which parses
it for structural correctness. Errors return Syntactic Validator
Feedback ($`\mathcal{F}^{s}`$) for regeneration; otherwise the rule
advances to semantic validation
\[Box [F-C](#A6.SS3 "F-C Validation and Self-Reflection ‣ Appendix F Example End-to-End Rule Generation and Validation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].

#### IV-D4 Semantic Validation

A valid rule proceeds to the Semantic Validator, where the CTI-Rule
Semantic Scorer \[see
Section [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\]
quantifies its functional similarity with $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$. The
Semantic Analysis LLM Agent, driven by this score, flags residual
inconsistencies, such as missing indicators, incorrect protocols, or
irrelevant payloads, and, if critical, formulates targeted feedback
($`\mathcal{F}^{f}`$) for the Rule Generator, prompting a revised
generation cycle
\[Box [F-C](#A6.SS3 "F-C Validation and Self-Reflection ‣ Appendix F Example End-to-End Rule Generation and Validation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/semantic_scorer_training.png)

Fig. 4: The correlation diagram shows the CTI–Rule Semantic Scorer’s
reliability in semantically mapping each CTI to its corresponding rule,
with highest similarity scores (Sigmoid $`\rightarrow`$ Softmax) on the
principal diagonal across 10 validation samples.

#### IV-D5 Performance Validation

The Performance Validator then checks runtime efficiency, including
regex use, rule complexity, match execution time, and mapping to
existing rules ($`\mathcal{R}^{e}_{i}`$). Inefficient rules are flagged
and routed back with performance-specific feedback ($`\mathcal{F}^{p}`$)
\[Box [F-D](#A6.SS4 "F-D Refined Output and Analyst Note ‣ Appendix F Example End-to-End Rule Generation and Validation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].

#### IV-D6 Cybersecurity Analyst Feedback

Validated rules and the consolidated Analyst Note
($`\mathcal{F}^{f}\cup\mathcal{F}^{p}`$) are forwarded to a
Cybersecurity Analyst for manual review and approval before deployment.
The analyst may also request regeneration under new constraints via
feedback ($`\mathcal{F}^{a}`$), enforcing organizational policy and
compliance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This modular, agent-driven design lets each component specialize in a
distinct function and enables iterative refinement. Combining LLM-driven
generation, parser-based syntax checks, functional-consistency scoring,
and performance profiling makes FALCON adaptable yet efficient at
producing high-quality IDS rules at scale.

## V Experiment & Evaluation

In this section, we present the experiments conducted to validate our
proposed FALCON framework. We designed three types of evaluation:
training and assessing the performance of the CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer
\[Sec.
[V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B Semantic Scorer Model Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
evaluation of Rule Generator LLM Agent \[Sec.
[V-C](#S5.SS3 "V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
and end-to-end qualitative validation of FALCON pipeline \[Sec.
[V-D](#S5.SS4 "V-D End-to-End FALCON Pipeline Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].

### V-A Data Description and Experiment Setup

To train and evaluate our CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer model and end-to-end
FALCON pipeline, we collected 4017 Snort⁴⁴ 4 Snort (Community):
[snort.org](https://snort.org) and 4587 YARA⁵⁵ 5 YARA:
[github.com/Yara-Rules/rules](https://github.com/Yara-Rules/rules) rules
($`\mathcal{R}_{i}`$) from open-source repositories and threat
intelligence datasets. Two CTI instances ($`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$) were
carefully generated for each rule, reflecting distinct but relevant
threat behavior and signature descriptions. Additionally, we generated a
list of relevant but outdated rules ($`\mathcal{R}_{i}^{e}`$) for each
rule to test out CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer as a retriever. This resulted
in 8034 Snort and 9174 YARA CTI-Rule pairs and 15217 snort and 25875
YARA deployed outdated rules ($`\mathcal{R}^{e}`$) for the retriever
assessment. The CTI-Rule dataset was then split into 90% for CTI-Rule
model training and 10% for testing (802 Snort and 916 YARA), ensuring
balanced representation across both types of IDS rules. Apart from
testing set, 60 Snort and 60 YARA were separately designed as validation
set for the overall pipeline’s qualitative evaluation. Each rule in the
validation set was categorized into one of three difficulty levels
(Easy, Medium, or Hard) based on complexity and length assessments
performed by Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) which are authors in our
case. These CTI and obsolete yet relevant IDS rules were designed to
simulate real-world use cases where FALCON must generate and validate
rules from novel CTI inputs and existing deployed rules. To simulate
diverse operational contexts, CTI was initially tested in both
semi-structured natural language and structured STIX
2.0 \[sadique2018automated\] formats. Our preliminary observations
indicated that semi-structured CTI led to more accurate generation of
IDS rules (example in
Section [IV](#S4 "IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
and we standardized subsequent evaluations on similar predefined CTI
format. However, the CTI schema remains flexible and can be adapted to
existing cybersecurity requirements, such as STIX or others. The
CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer models were built on top of pre-trained
embedding models and trained using contrastive learning (details in
Section
[IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection"))
with different hyperparameter configurations, and early stopping based
on validation loss. This selection is intentional, as our findings with
LLM embeddings were poor and inefficient. All training was performed on
six NVIDIA H200 GPUs, and dataset, code, preliminary, and complete
experimental results are reported in the
repository[1](#footnote1 "footnote 1 ‣ Abstract ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").

### V-B Semantic Scorer Model Evaluation

To validate our answer to RQ-2
\[Section [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C FALCON CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer Model ‣ IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
we benchmark the CTI-Rule Semantic Scorer against four baselines across
its two roles, retrieval and ground-truth-free validation
\[Table [II](#S5.T2 "TABLE II ‣ V-B Semantic Scorer Model Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].
The Consistency columns establish its validity as a validator: lacking a
reference rule at test time, we check that scoring a generated rule
against its CTI (CTI$`\to`$G) tracks scoring it against the ground-truth
rule (GT$`\to`$G), via their mean absolute gap
($`|\Delta|\!\downarrow`$) and correlation ($`r\!\uparrow`$);
per-platform scatter plots of this CTI$`\to`$G vs GT$`\to`$G agreement
appear in
Appendix [I-B](#A9.SS2 "I-B Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Validation ‣ Appendix I Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Analysis ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").
The Retriever columns assess retrieval of relevant deployed rules by
Recall@10 (R@10) and Mean Average Precision (MAP). The Semantic columns
measure a generated rule’s alignment with its CTI by diagonal recall
(S.Rec), i.e., whether the principal-diagonal score is highest in its
row, and a thresholded F1 (Thr) at the optimal post-scaling threshold.
Per column, best shaded green and second-best blue.

### V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation

RQ-1 and RQ-3.
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")
jointly evaluates rule-generation feasibility (RQ-1) and self-reflective
refinement (RQ-3) over 18 LLMs, 14 general-purpose models across Small
(S, 3–4B), Medium (M, 8–30B), Large (L, 32–49B), and Extra-Large (XL,
117–128B) scales plus four cyber-security fine-tuned models (Cyb), for
both Snort (NIDS) and YARA (HIDS). Each model is run in two modes:
Single, a one-shot generation with no validator feedback (the RQ-1
baseline), and Chain, the full validator-chained self-reflective loop of
Section [IV](#S4 "IV FALCON Framework ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")
in which syntactic, semantic, and performance feedback drives iterative
regeneration (RQ-3). Generated rules are scored by our CTI-Rule scorer
(sigmoid functional alignment), RAGAS \[es2024ragas\] (OpenAI-embedding
cosine), and BERT-F1 \[zhang2019bertscore\] (baseline-rescaled
BERTScore), each against the input CTI (CTI vs Gen) and the ground-truth
rule (Gen vs GT); Pass counts generations clearing all three validators
(out of 802 Snort / 916 YARA). To test whether agentic reasoning adds
value *on top of* self-reflection, the five reasoning-capable models
(Qwen3-4B/14B/32B, Nemotron-Super-49B, and GPT-OSS-117B) are
additionally run with thinking enabled and disabled (Th on/off).

For RQ-1, even in one-shot Single mode, models across all scales
transform heterogeneous CTI into relevant, deployable rules, with the
CTI-Rule score holding a stable $`\approx\!0.72`$ where lexical BERT-F1
swings widely. For RQ-3, Chain consistently raises the Pass rate over
Single (e.g., Qwen3-32B Snort $`451\!\to\!649`$, Mistral-Medium YARA
$`597\!\to\!912`$), confirming that structured validator feedback yields
measurable gains over one-shot generation. Enabling thinking on the five
reasoning-capable models produces only marginal, inconsistent changes on
top of Chain, indicating that the validator-driven self-reflection,
rather than reasoning alone, is the primary driver of improvement.

### V-D End-to-End FALCON Pipeline Evaluation

To address RQ-3, i.e., whether an LLM can interpret validator feedback
to improve a generated rule, we close the loop between the validation
and generation phases and re-run the same 10% evaluation split (802
Snort, 916 YARA) with the best-performing LLM in each size category
\[Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
plotting the refined semantic score (orange) against one-shot generation
(blue) for the runs that required refinement
\[Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].
Aggregated across all matched model$`\times`$family$`\times`$perspective
configurations, chain-validator refinement raises the semantic score by
$`+0.130`$ ($`+18.0\%`$) over single-shot, whereas enabling agentic
reasoning shifts it by a negligible $`\approx\!0\%`$ ($`-0.1\%`$
all-validator, $`+0.7\%`$ syntax-only)
\[Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
confirming that the validator loop, not reasoning, drives the gain. This
lift is measured from the initial one-shot rule, including sub-threshold
cases, to the refined output; accepted rules themselves cluster near the
validator thresholds. A per-validator breakdown of the single-shot
failures rescued by the chain, together with the thinking on/off
comparison, appears in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Validator Ablation and Failure Mode Analysis ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").

To corroborate the quantitative results, we qualitatively assess
end-to-end feasibility on 60 isolated validation samples. Three
cyber-security Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) independently rate 60
generated rule on a Likert scale: non-match (0), syntactically correct
(1), semantically correct (2), and performance-optimized (3)
\[Table [V](#S5.T5 "TABLE V ‣ V-D End-to-End FALCON Pipeline Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].
Scores are aggregated per difficulty category and normalized to
$`[0\text{--}1]`$ to measure consensus. We observe 84% inter-rater
agreement, indicating the consistency and reliability of FALCON.

|                 |            |       |         |         |
|-----------------|------------|-------|---------|---------|
| Medium-Platform | Difficulty | Llama | Mistral | Granite |
| NIDS-Snort      | Easy       | 1.00  | 1.00    | 1.00    |
|                 | Medium     | 0.98  | 0.98    | 1.00    |
|                 | Hard       | 0.95  | 0.93    | 1.00    |
| HIDS-YARA       | Easy       | 0.95  | 0.98    | 1.00    |
|                 | Medium     | 0.86  | 0.86    | 0.92    |

### V-E Discussion

From experimental results, we draw following observations:

(1) Retrieval is competitive but validation is not. On the retrieval
task, the CTI-Rule model attains near-perfect Recall@10 and MAP
\[Table [II](#S5.T2 "TABLE II ‣ V-B Semantic Scorer Model Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
but sparse and dense baselines (TF-IDF, BM25, RAGAS) remain close
because deployed rules and their CTIs share substantial token overlap.
Retrieval is therefore best served by an efficient ensemble (sparse +
dense) re-ranker. The picture inverts for ground-truth-free validation:
lexical and embedding baselines collapse and the CTI-Rule scorer becomes
indispensable, as seen in the Consistency and thresholded-F1 columns of
Table [II](#S5.T2 "TABLE II ‣ V-B Semantic Scorer Model Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection").

(2) Larger models has more coverage (RQ-1). Across the full suite
\[Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
models from 3B to 128B all produce syntactically, semantically, and
operationally valid rules, but the number of CTIs successfully
translated (Pass) grows with model scale: the largest model,
Mistral-Medium (128B), clears the most ($`800/802`$ Snort, $`912/916`$
YARA), whereas the small 3–4B models (e.g., Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.2)
translate markedly fewer, especially on YARA. Because every accepted
rule must clear the same validator thresholds, post-pass similarity
scores cluster in a narrow band; the discriminating quantity is
therefore *coverage* (Pass), not score magnitude.

(3) CTI-Rule scorer similarity is logical (RQ-2). Comparing
semantic-similarity metrics, RAGAS tends to overestimate and BERT-F1 to
underestimate alignment, and both fluctuate sharply across models and
rule families. Our CTI-Rule scorer instead stays stable
($`\approx\!0.72`$) and returns nearly identical values for the
CTI-vs-generated and generated-vs-ground-truth columns (e.g., $`0.72`$
vs $`0.73`$), whereas RAGAS ($`\approx\!0.70`$ vs $`\approx\!0.95`$) and
BERT-F1 ($`\approx\!-0.15`$ vs $`\approx\!0.46`$) diverge widely between
the two
\[Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\].
the same behavior appears in all four evaluation graphs
\[Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
where our model traces nearly coincident trends (green line) across both
comparisons. If the scorer captured surface lexical patterns rather than
latent logic, the two comparisons ($`1^{st}`$ vs $`2^{nd}`$ and
$`3^{rd}`$ vs $`4^{th}`$) would diverge, as they do for RAGAS and
BERT-F1. Formally, if both CTI and rule are projected onto the same
latent distribution, the CTI-to-generated and generated-to-ground-truth
similarities should coincide, since the CTI-to-ground-truth score is
unity
$`\big[\text{sim}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{c}(\mathcal{C}_{i}),\,\mathcal{E}_{r}(\mathcal{R}_{i})\right)=\text{sim}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{r}(\mathcal{R}_{i}),\,\mathcal{E}_{r}(\mathcal{R}_{i}^{gt})\right)`$,
where
$`\text{sim}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{c}(\mathcal{C}_{i}),\,\mathcal{E}_{r}(\mathcal{R}_{i}^{gt})\right)=1\big]`$.
This consistency is strong evidence that the scorer represents logical
relationships in latent space rather than matching lexical patterns, a
crucial finding toward explainable, functionally meaningful evaluation
of IDS rule generation.

(4) Self-reflection matters for complex rules (RQ-3). Snort rules are
comparatively simple, and LLMs often pass on the first shot, so the gain
from one-shot (Single) to validator-chained refinement (Chain) is
modest. YARA rules are more complex and frequently need 2–3 refinement
iterations
\[Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
producing large Single$`\to`$Chain increases in Pass
\[Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\]
(e.g., Mistral-Medium $`597\!\to\!912`$ and Qwen3-32B $`648\!\to\!879`$
on YARA, versus near-flat Snort). Aggregated over all matched
configurations, refinement lifts the semantic score by $`+18.0\%`$ over
one-shot
\[Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
confirming that directed validator feedback yields measurable gains and
supplies the generation trajectory LLMs lack for complex formats. By
contrast, enabling agentic reasoning on the five reasoning-capable
models contributes a negligible $`\approx\!0\%`$ on average
\[Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
indicating that validator loop is the primary driver.

(5) Knowledge $`\approx`$ coverage; refinement $`\approx`$ quality.
Coverage scales with model size (observation 2) because larger models
hold more of the threat- and format-specific knowledge needed to
interpret a CTI and emit a valid rule. The *quality* of accepted rules,
by contrast, is size-agnostic: with self-reflective refinement, models
of widely different sizes reach comparable Snort and YARA scores for a
given CTI and its retrieved rules
\[Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
as seen from Granite across its 3/8/30B variants. Scale therefore
supplies the context knowledge that governs how many CTIs a model can
translate, while the validator loop governs how good each accepted rule
is.

(6) Domain fine-tuning substitutes scaling. Cyber-tuned models confirm
that coverage tracks domain knowledge rather than raw parameter count.
Within their 7–8B class, the stronger ones match or beat same-size
general models
\[Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\];
more strikingly, on the simpler Snort format the domain-tuned
Foundation-Sec (8B) reaches $`797`$ Pass, rivaling Mistral-Medium-128B
($`800`$) and surpassing far larger general models such as Qwen3-32B and
Nemotron-49B, i.e., injected domain knowledge offsets a $`16\times`$
size gap. Scale’s broader knowledge still prevails on the more complex
YARA ($`912`$ for Mistral-Medium vs $`\sim\!830`$ for the domain-tuned
8B). Hence domain-alignment, can help limit scaling for bounded
generation tasks.

## VI Conclusion

We presented FALCON, an agentic framework that transforms heterogeneous
CTI into deployable Snort and YARA rules via retrieval, generation, and
self-reflective syntactic, semantic, and performance validation. Its
core is a novel ground-truth-free CTI-Rule semantic scorer that serves a
dual retrieval-and-validation role. Across 18 LLMs we show that
validator-driven self-reflection yields measurable quality gains
($`+18\%`$), largest for complex YARA rules, while agentic reasoning
adds little, and that coverage is governed by domain knowledge.
Achieving 84% inter-rater agreement with SOC analysts, FALCON makes
real-time, explainable, ground-truth-free IDS-rule automation feasible;
future work targets proprietary CTI/rule corpora and SOAR integration
for continuous, large-scale refinement.

## Appendix B Threats to Validity

Construct. FALCON uses the learned scorer $`\Phi`$ both as the semantic
validator and as a headline metric, so any systematic bias in $`\Phi`$
propagates to retrieval and validation alike; we mitigate this through
the CTI$`\to`$G vs GT$`\to`$G consistency analysis and independent SME
ratings, but $`\Phi`$ is not an external ground truth, and Pass depends
on the chosen validator thresholds.

Internal. Part of the Single$`\to`$Chain gain could arise from
resampling rather than directed feedback; we do not fully separate the
two, since each Chain run couples additional regenerations with the
feedback signal.

External. Evaluation covers open-source Snort and YARA under a
standardized semi-structured CTI format and a fixed LLM suite. Hence,
generalization to other engines (e.g., Suricata, Sigma), proprietary
rule/CTI corpora, and noisier real-world CTI remains untested.

Scope. Consistent with our hypothesis
(Section [III](#S3 "III Problem Formulation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")),
we assume each CTI carries sufficient signature/behavior information for
rule generation; adversarial crafted or information-poor CTI both
violate this assumption, and FALCON’s behavior in such cases is out of
scope. The quality of the LLM-generated validator feedback is likewise
orthogonal to this study and not separately analyzed.

Conclusion. Most configurations are run once and the qualitative study
rests on three SME raters (the authors) over 60 samples; broader,
independent replication would strengthen the statistical claims.

## Appendix F Example End-to-End Rule Generation and Validation

This section provides a complete, worked-out example of the FALCON
generative and validation pipeline using a YARA rule generation task.
The progression demonstrates how heterogeneous CTI is contextualized
against a retrieved rule, synthesized into a candidate rule using
target-specific instructions, evaluated via serial validators, and
refined using self-reflective feedback (answering RQ-1, RQ-2, and RQ-3).

### F-A Input and Retrieval

The generation process begins with unstructured CTI. This excerpt
describes an evolved Mirai variant.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Using the semantic scorer, FALCON retrieves structurally linked rules
from the deployed rule base to supply context, helping prevent redundant
“rule bloat”.

### F-B Candidate Generation

The Rule Generator LLM Agent receives a rigid system prompt configuring
its role, constraints, and target platform as extracted from the
experiment code.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The LLM outputs an initial candidate rule. In this sample, the syntax is
valid, but the condition block mistakenly drops the new C2 string
reference constraint (\$c2).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### F-C Validation and Self-Reflection

The candidate $`\mathcal{R}^{(0)}_{i}`$ passes through short-circuit
serial validation. Here, it passes syntax, but the semantic validator
flags functional misalignment because the CTI semantic elements and the
missing \$c2 drop the score to $`0.62`$, which is below the passing
threshold of $`0.7107`$. The chain-loop builds structured user feedback.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### F-D Refined Output and Analyst Note

Conditioned on this strict feedback, the LLM refines the rule condition
to include the missing constraint. This second iteration yields a rule
that fulfills the syntax, functional semantics (similarity
$`\geq 0.7107`$ and surpassing $`\epsilon_{i}^{\max}`$), and performance
validation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On successful cycle completion, performance checks (complexity/latency
constraints) are unified with semantic checks for final human sign-off.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix G Dataset Description

This section presents the empirical distributions and profiles of the
dataset used to train and evaluate the framework. Across the evaluation
corpus, the dataset characteristics are analyzed along three central
dimensions: the frequency of negative distractors paired with each CTI
profile (Decoys per CTI”), the linguistic volume of the input threat
intelligence (CTI length”) , and the syntactic footprint of the formal
detection constraints (Rule length”) categorized by ground-truth (gold”)
and outdated context (“decoy”) signatures. These structural properties
are mapped distinctively across the 802 network-based (Snort) and 916
host-based (YARA) threat profiles to ensure robust diversity across both
detection mediums.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/data_description_appendix.png)

Fig. 7: Distribution of the dataset for Snort (top row; 802 total CTIs)
and YARA (bottom row; 916 total CTIs) platforms. The metrics trace the
distribution of paired decoys per CTI (left) , the character length
metrics of the source CTI text (middle) , and a comparative character
length breakdown between ground-truth (gold) and legacy context (decoy)
rulesets (right).

## Appendix H Validator Ablation and Failure Mode Analysis

This section presents an ablation study analyzing 11,719 single-shot
baseline failures and evaluates the corrective capacity of FALCON’s
feedback loop across 184 model runs.

Programmatic syntax flaws represent the primary barrier to automated
rule deployment, accounting for 95% (11,100 rules) of all single-shot
rejections across the entire evaluation corpus. Specifically, Snort
baseline failures are composed of 91% syntax (1,899), 8% semantic (169),
and 1% performance (13) errors. YARA baseline failures demonstrate an
even higher syntactic fragility, skewing at 95% syntax (9,201), 4%
semantic (341), and 1% performance (96) rejections.

Activating the validation chain effectively counteracts this structural
fragility by translating execution errors into actionable adjustments.
The loop successfully rescues 34.5% of failing cases (717/2,081) for
Snort and 51.5% of failures (4,965/9,638) for complex YARA rule
structures. Across all configurations, externalized feedback delivers an
absolute mean lift of +0.130 (+18.0%) to the final pass_all capability
gate over a mean convergence profile of 2.357 iterations, ensuring a
100% win-rate over single-shot baselines.

Conversely, an ablation isolating test-time model reasoning (“thinking”)
reveals a negligible impact on rule viability: averaged over all matched
configurations
\[Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-C Rule Generator LLM Agent Evaluation ‣ V Experiment & Evaluation ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")\],
toggling thinking shifts the semantic score by only $`-0.001`$
($`-0.1\%`$) over all-three-pass rules and $`+0.006`$ ($`+0.7\%`$) over
syntax-pass rules. This confirms that compiler-driven external loop
context—rather than internal token generation reasoning depth—is the
definitive driver of deployable signature quality.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/validator_ablation_study_appendix.png)

Fig. 8: Comprehensive breakdown of single-shot baseline failure types
across 18 evaluated language models for Snort (left) and YARA (right)
platforms. The horizontal bars track baseline rejections by the specific
validation component that blocked deployment, detailing the distribution
of programmatic syntax flaws (orange), semantic functional mismatches
(blue), and operational performance overheads (green).

## Appendix I Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Analysis

### I-A Embedding Separability and Latent Space Alignment Shift

To visualize how CFT restructures the cross-modal latent space,
Figure [9](#A9.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ I-A Embedding Separability and Latent Space Alignment Shift ‣ Appendix I Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Analysis ‣ FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection")
maps our models against their pretrained foundation baselines, tracking
true-match alignment (Diagonal Mean) against false-match convergence
(Off-Diagonal Mean). Out-of-the-box baselines like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and
e5-base-v2 exhibit severe representation collapse in the upper-right
quadrant, combining high diagonal similarity ($`\approx 0.90`$) with
massive off-diagonal inflation ($`\approx 0.80`$). Similarly, pretrained
all-mpnet-base-v2 slightly reduces false matches ($`\approx 0.32`$) but
suffers from depressed diagonal alignment ($`\approx 0.56`$).

Contrastive fine-tuning drives a dramatic migration toward the ideal
top-left corner, compressing off-diagonal false matches to a tight
window ($`0.01`$ to $`0.15`$) while isolating true-match diagonal
similarity between $`0.85`$ and $`0.96`$. Notably, Bi-Encoder variants
(blue markers) demonstrate stronger true-match preservation over
Dual-Encoder configurations (orange markers), confirming their superior
capacity for context-aware retrieval and zero-day validation.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/cti-rule_model_axis_point.png)

Fig. 9: Embedding separability mapping out-of-the-box models against our
for Snort (left) and YARA (right) in cross-modal spaces. The coordinate
vector illustrates the migration from uncalibrated baselines (marked
with ’X’) to the optimized top-left quadrant. Maximizing vertical
position ensures stronger true-match alignment, while minimizing
horizontal position minimizes false-positive cross-modal matching.

### I-B Cross-Modal Latent Space Consistency Validation

Here we present the trained semantic scorer as a ground-truth-free
validator by comparing $`\text{score}(\text{CTI},\text{GenRule})`$
against $`\text{score}(\text{GTRule},\text{GenRule})`$. A reliable
scorer’s evaluation points should lie along the ideal $`y=x`$ diagonal
line.

On the network-based Snort platform, the CTI-Rule scorer hugs the
diagonal closely, achieving a Pearson correlation of $`r=0.888`$ and a
minimal mean absolute score gap of $`|\Delta|=0.023`$. Baseline metrics
reveal severe semantic distortions, with BERT-F1
($`r=0.428,|\Delta|=0.355`$) and RAGAS ($`r=0.511,|\Delta|=0.269`$)
failing to capture consistent cross-modal alignment.

For host-based YARA rules, our scorer demonstrates an even tighter
calibration, reaching $`r=0.974`$ and $`|\Delta|=0.012`$. Lexical
tracking via BM25 correlates strongly on YARA
($`r=0.946,|\Delta|=0.030`$) due to identical structural identifier
reuse, but collapses when evaluated against the abstract prose of Snort
configurations ($`r=0.743,|\Delta|=0.198`$). This cross-paradigm
stability confirms our regularized latent space measures true functional
alignment rather than surface-level token matching.

![Refer to caption](2508.18684v2/semantic_scorer_eval.png)

Fig. 10: Cross-modal consistency evaluation mapping
$`\text{metric}(\text{CTI},\text{GenRule})`$ vs.
$`\text{metric}(\text{GTRule},\text{GenRule})`$ for Snort (left) and
YARA (right) platforms. The scatter plots illustrate how closely each
metric’s proxy score conforms to the ideal $`y=x`$ diagonal agreement
line. The lower bar charts quantify performance via the mean absolute
score gap ($`|\Delta|`$, lower is better) and the Pearson correlation
coefficient ($`r`$, higher is better).
````
